cia-0000136206: A CIA cable dated 6 May 1954 deals with the availability of F-47 planes, called critical to the operation in the cable's own heading, in files since declassified. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136306: Cable from Lincoln for Cadick and Broadfrost an Order: re Strike Mission is a declassified CIA cable dated 1954. The catalog title is unusually informative for this series: a sender signing as Lincoln, two recipients named Cadick and Broadfrost, and a message that gives an order about a strike mission. Names of that style were the working code names used inside agency traffic. The catalog adds nothing about the mission or its outcome. The cable survives as a brief piece of operational traffic, released through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000136706: Dated 6 February 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified files of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was in final training, its April landing in Cuba about ten weeks off. The catalog gives this item no subject heading. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the brigade's February records from the operation's last stretch of preparation.
cia-06786606: COVERAGE OF THE SAIGON-GIA DINH SITUATION FOR THE PERIOD 0800 3 FEBRUARY TO 21, a CIA document. The Saigon coverage. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-06841006: LIBERIA: WAR AND PEACE THROUGH TAYLOR'S EYES, a CIA assessment. The Liberian view. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
conrad-mirror-of-sea-1906:
The Mirror of the Sea, published in 1906, is Conrad's book of memoir-essays on the sailing life he had left behind. After twenty years in the merchant service, he wrote of ships and the sea as a man speaks of a lost home.

The essays take up anchors, storms, the character of famous ships, and the fellowship of crews. 'The Fine Art' praises seamanship as a craft of hand and judgment. There is no plot here, only memory refined into prose of great beauty. Sailors and landsmen alike have kept it in print as the classic elegy for the age of sail.
constitution-brunei-2006: Brunei's Constitution, amended 2006, frames its absolute sultanate. The Sultan holds full power. The Tower library holds the full text. It kept a sultan supreme. Oil funded. Crown ruled. Law obeyed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-serbia-2006: Serbia's 2006 Constitution frames its republic after Yugoslavia. It claims Kosovo. The Tower library holds the full text. It stood alone. Federation broke. State claimed. Law stood. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
contra-l-alchimia-e-gli-alchimisti-palin: An Italian voice rose against the alchemists in 1606. The palinode recanted the Argonautica's claims. The anti-alchemy polemic. Its pages add to the record of the past. This book preserves that rare tract. Kept for readers.
contro-l-alchimia-e-gli-alchimisti-palin: Contro l'alchimia e gli alchimisti palinodia, 1606. Another edition. This book preserves that polemic. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-06:
Number six of The Equinox followed in September 1911, the autumn half of the journal's year. Crowley kept his twice-yearly vow, and the numbers grew in size and range. London's occult readers knew the fat white volumes well by sight.

More rites and holy texts make their first bow in print in this issue. Essays and reviews around them show the order at talk with its age. Each number is a season's harvest of the young movement at work. This one documents the movement in its rich middle growth. The harvest here is rite, song, and polemic in turn.
dampier-voyages-vol1-1906:
William Dampier, an English buccaneer with a naturalist's eye, circled the globe in the late seventeenth century. Volume One of John Masefield's 1906 edition centers on his A New Voyage Round the World of 1697. Dampier was the first Englishman to explore Australia's coast.

Sailing with pirates in the Pacific, he still found time to note winds, plants, animals, and peoples. His plain, exact style shaped English travel writing and fed Swift and Defoe. Masefield, himself a sailor-poet, edits with love. Dampier's double life, pirate and pioneer of science, makes the volume a lasting pleasure. His word lists for native tongues were among the first printed in English.
dampier-voyages-vol2-1906:
Volume Two of Masefield's edition of Dampier's Voyages continues the buccaneer-naturalist's writings. Dampier's later works include his discourse on trade winds and his voyage to New Holland in 1699. The Royal Navy had by then given the old pirate a ship of his own.

His wind charts served sailors for a century, and his account of Australia's west coast was the first in English. Dampier describes strange animals and plants with a pioneer's patience. Masefield adds the supplement and the remaining voyages to complete the set. The volume shows why scientists, not only sailors, honored Dampier's name.
doe-osti-17011135-vitrification-of-hanfo: Turning Hanford's radioactive sludge into glass got its technical record, and this DOE report covers tank 241-AW-106 vitrification. The pages detail the melt and the simulant tests. The nuclear legacy gets locked in glass. The process was proven. The glass was proven.
doe-osti-3563284-final-technical-report-: DE-SC0022206 got technical-finalled, and this DOE final covers the report. The pages detail the final findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was technical. The closeout was researcher. The DE-SC0022206 were final. The researchers were closeout.
dreyer-history-planetary-systems-1906:
J. L. E. Dreyer published his History of the Planetary Systems in 1906. The subtitle carries the story from Thales to Kepler in one volume. Dreyer was a Danish astronomer and a leading historian of astronomy.

Greek spheres and epicycles give way slowly to medieval refinements here. Ptolemy's system receives full treatment as ancient astronomy's summit. Copernicus, Tycho, and Kepler then rebuild the heavens in the final chapters. Dreyer edited Tycho Brahe's complete works, which deepens his later chapters. The book became the classic history of ancient and medieval astronomy. Two thousand years of cosmology unfold in his single, lucid volume for students.
dunsany-time-and-the-gods-1906:
Dunsany's gods met their master in Time and the Gods, the sequel of 1906. Time stalks the deities of Pegana in these tales, and one by one they learn they can die. The cycle deepens the myth world of his first book.

Kings pray, gods war and fade, and a green slave god rises as old faiths fall. Dunsany writes of the death of gods with a poet's calm and awe. The book taught later fantasy how to let its gods end in beauty and in sorrow. It is the sadder and greater of the two Pegana books.
ehrlich-collected-studies-immunity-vol1-:
Paul Ehrlich was a German doctor and chemist who studied how the body defends itself against disease. Charles Bolduan translated his research papers into English. This first volume of the collected studies was published in 1906.

The papers present Ehrlich's side-chain theory, his picture of how cells make antibodies to fight toxins. With his co-workers he studied hemolysins, substances in blood that break down red blood cells. The contents list experiments on receptors, immune sera, and the chemical basis of immunity. This research laid groundwork for immunology, the science of body defense, and for modern drug design as well.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-06: Volume six finds Montaigne questioning the ways of his age. He probes cruelty, justice, and the hollow claims of custom. The essayist's fairness feels strikingly modern. A brave and independent mind in a violent and cruel century.
europmc-pmc10037406:
Kim, Kim, and Chung review how DNA escapes from mitochondria and switches on an immune alarm pathway, in a 2023 paper. DNA normally stays inside the cell nucleus and its mitochondria, the cell's powerhouses. DNA found loose in the cell is read as a danger sign, much like the DNA of an invading germ.

The authors trace the routes by which mitochondrial DNA leaks out. They explain how a sensor called cGAS then triggers the STING pathway and an immune response. The review links this alarm to infection defense, aging, and disease.
europmc-pmc10322706:
Kim and a large team reported a new drug in 2023 that blocks KRAS, a protein often changed in cancer. KRAS acts like a switch that tells cells to grow. When the switch sticks on, tumours can form. Past drugs could block just one form of the switch, called G12C.

The new drug from Kim binds KRAS when the switch is off, and it spares two close kin proteins. It stopped the switch from turning on in tests on many changed forms. Growth slowed only in cancer cells that held a changed KRAS. In mice, the drug shrank tumours with no loss of body weight.
europmc-pmc10860306:
Khan, Fatima, Aisha, and Malik review why cancer drugs stop working in this 2024 paper. Resistance is a core hurdle in cancer care. Some tumours resist from the start, while others learn to resist over time. Changes in genes, gene use, proteins, energy use, and the tumour's surroundings can all drive it.

The review maps these escape routes at the level of molecules and cells. It weighs pairing drugs, which can work better but often adds side effects. Newer options get close attention, above all precision immune therapy, which trains the immune system on the patient's own tumour. Stem cell based options are also discussed. The authors note that immune therapy is tailored to each person, which limits its reach for now.
europmc-pmc11116106:
M Bran and colleagues built a chemistry agent on a large language model in this 2024 paper. Large language models are AI systems trained on vast text that can reason and write. They perform well in many domains but struggle with chemistry problems. They also cannot reach outside knowledge or lab tools on their own.

Their agent, ChemCrow, links the model GPT-4 to 18 expert-designed chemistry tools. The agent planned and carried out the making of an insect repellent and three organocatalysts, the authors report. Organocatalysts are carbon-based molecules that speed reactions. It also guided the discovery of a novel chromophore, a molecule that absorbs light in a useful way. Judges, both AI and human experts, rated its work across a diverse task set. The authors aim to aid experts and lower barriers for non-experts.
europmc-pmc1142306:
Ribble, Goldstein, Norris, and Shellman present a simple plate-based method to count dying cells in this 2005 paper. Apoptosis is programmed cell death, a routine measure in biological studies. Existing counting methods involve multiple, sometimes cell-damaging steps and cannot score live, dead, and apoptotic cells at once. False positives add further error.

Their modified stain assay runs entirely in a 96-well plate, a standard lab tray with many small wells. It adapts a classic two-dye method using ethidium bromide and acridine orange. The team compared it with the conventional method on suspension cells and adherent cells, under normal and death-inducing conditions. Results matched the conventional method for both cell types. The authors conclude the plate format keeps accuracy while removing transfer steps that damage cells.
europmc-pmc11920006:
GBD 2021 Adolescent BMI Collaborators mapped child and teen weight trends in 2025. Excess weight in youth raises later risk of chronic disease. Global action still lags, and measures vary by country. Clear numbers help set targets and direct resources.

Models drew on 1,321 data sources from 180 countries and territories. They tracked overweight and obesity from 1990 to 2021. Forecasts then extend the trends to 2050. Results split by age, sex, and place for close reading. GBD 2021 Adolescent BMI Collaborators give planners a long view of a growing problem. Between 1990 and 2021, combined rates doubled across childhood and teen years. Obesity alone tripled in that span.
europmc-pmc1287506:
Meyer and Paulay measured error rates for DNA barcoding in cowrie snails in 2005. Barcoding promises fast species identification from short DNA tags. Few fully sampled groups had tested that promise. Cowries, a diverse marine snail group, gave a tough test.

Against a known family tree, the best identification error was 4 percent. In partly known groups, error rates hit about 17 percent. The expected gap between within-species and between-species variation overlapped heavily. Using only traditional species names doubled the errors. Meyer shows barcoding works best where sampling is complete. In partly known groups, species calls rest on cutoff values set in advance.
europmc-pmc1409806:
Epstein-Barr virus hides in human cells for life, and it makes tiny bits of RNA called microRNAs. Cai and co-authors counted those bits in 2006 and found at least 17 of them. They sit in two groups on the virus genome. One group is strong in skin-like cells, the other in immune B cells.

Levels of each group shift with the stage of infection and tissue type. Cai also checked a kin virus in monkeys, split from this one long ago. It keeps at least 16 such bits, and seven match closely. That match suggests these small RNAs do real work in the virus life cycle.
europmc-pmc1479806:
Reactive oxygen species are harsh forms of oxygen made in cells. Waris and Ahsan reviewed their role in cancer and chronic disease in 2006. These species can scar DNA, causing changes that may start cancer growth. Some cancer-causing agents work in part by raising their levels.

High levels of these species, with weak defenses against them, show up in many cancers. They also play a part in diabetes and nerve decay diseases. Waris notes they sway core cell acts like growth, self-killing, and aging. Grasping how they carry signals inside cells could open new drug routes, the review argues.
europmc-pmc1500806:
A seaweed extract may block the virus that causes cervical cancer. Buck and co-authors found in 2006 that carrageenan, a thickener from red algae, stops human papillomavirus cold. Lab tests covered a broad range of sexually spread types.

The extract blocked half of infections at doses of a few billionths of a gram per milliliter. That is about a thousand times stronger than its effect on herpes or HIV. It works mainly by stopping virus particles from latching onto cells, mimicking a natural cell glue. Buck notes some shop products with carrageenan blocked the virus even diluted a million-fold. Trials in people come next.
europmc-pmc1592506:
African health workers often feel driven yet thwarted. Mathauer and Imhoff studied motivation in Benin and Kenya in 2006, interviewing 99 doctors and nurses in rural facilities. A staffing crisis grips health systems across the continent.

Workers said professional conscience and vocation guided them strongly. Frustration grew when missing supplies and tools blocked them from doing their jobs well. Some management tools made things worse, applied badly or unfairly. Money alone was not the answer: the pair found motivation hinges on a mix of pay and non-financial incentives, plus sound management practice.
europmc-pmc1626106:
Even single-celled bacteria can run programs that kill some of their own. Engelberg-Kulka and co-authors reviewed two such systems in 2006. Programmed cell death was long thought a trait of many-celled life.

One system, mazEF, pairs a toxin with its antidote in the chromosomes of many bacteria. When triggered, the toxin kills the cell. The second system works in Bacillus subtilis during spore formation. Two gene sets, skf and sdp, kill a share of the sporulating cells. Engelberg-Kulka relates both systems to ways bacterial groups act like multicellular organisms, sacrificing some cells for the whole.
europmc-pmc1629006:
Drug labels may claim benefits that patients themselves report. A 2006 draft guidance from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, with sister FDA centers, sets how such claims are judged. A patient-reported outcome is any health measure that comes straight from the patient, with no doctor interpreting it.

Such measures range from a symptom, like headache relief, to quality of life across body, mind, and social life. The guidance explains how the FDA reviews these instruments in trials. It tells sponsors how to build and document them, so labeling claims rest on sound patient evidence.
europmc-pmc1794406:
Picci reviewed osteosarcoma in 2007, a rare bone cancer whose tumor cells directly form immature bone. It makes up only 0.2 percent of all malignant tumors, with about three cases per million people each year. Most cases arise in the long bones of patients aged 10 to 25 years.

Diagnosis and planning rely on plain X-rays, CT and MRI scans, angiography, and bone scans. Decades ago every patient faced amputation, yet the cure rate stayed under 10 percent. Modern care at specialist centers pairs surgery with chemotherapy before and after the operation. For localized disease, which covers 80 percent of cases at onset, cure now reaches 60 to 70 percent. Over 90 percent of patients keep the limb, while axial tumors and spread at onset cure only about 30 percent.
europmc-pmc1804206:
Papenfort, Vogel and co-authors found in 2006 how Salmonella bacteria clear their own messages during membrane stress. When misfolded proteins jam the outer membrane, a stress factor called sigmaE switches on. It swiftly lowers the messenger RNAs for major outer membrane proteins, freeing the folding machinery.

The missing agents were two small non-coding RNAs, RybB and MicA, both switched on by sigmaE. Tracking RNA decay in living cells showed RybB speeds the breakdown of many outer membrane protein messages at once. MicA appears to handle one key message, ompA, on its own. In calm cells the pair forms a surveillance loop that keeps the membrane in balance and holds sigmaE itself in check. Their work gives the stress response a concrete molecular mechanism.
europmc-pmc1906806:
So, Tschopp and co-authors piloted in 2007 a targeted anti-inflammatory drug for acute gout attacks. Gout flares when urate crystals inflame a joint. The crystals make immune cells release interleukin-1 beta through a sensor complex called the inflammasome, and blocking interleukin-1 helps related inherited fever diseases.

In mice, blocking interleukin-1 stopped crystal-driven immune cell buildup in the body cavity, while blocking a rival signal, TNF, did nothing. The team then gave anakinra, an interleukin-1 blocker, to ten gout patients who could not take or had failed standard drugs. Each received 100 milligrams daily for three days. All ten patients responded rapidly, and no adverse effects appeared. The authors call interleukin-1 blockade an effective option, while noting a controlled trial must confirm it.
europmc-pmc2002206:
Twentyman and Luscombe studied in 1987 how to use the MTT assay well, a colour test for living cells. Living cells turn a soluble yellow dye into an insoluble purple product, called formazan. Colour strength then shows cell growth and drug response. The authors varied solvent, dye amount, timing and leftover medium to find stable conditions.

Dimethyl sulfoxide dissolved the product best, even with medium left in the wells. Medium changed the colour spectrum, but volumes of 1 to 10 microlitres mattered little. Larger volumes lowered readings, then raised them through cloudiness above 40 microlitres. Colour rose in a straight line with cell number. The team adopted four hours as standard. Results matched direct cell counts for mouse tumour cells.
europmc-pmc2094306:
Nehme and co-workers built a fruit fly model in 2007 for gut infections by the bacterium Serratia marcescens. This microbe infects many hosts, including people, when defences are weak. Injected straight into a fly's body cavity, it kills within a day and shrugs off immune attack. That resistance needs the bacterial surface coat, called O-antigen. The team instead fed bacteria to flies, mimicking food-borne infection.

Eaten bacteria crossed the gut wall, passing through intestinal cells, and flies died only after six days. Two defences acted together against this slower route. An antimicrobial response in the gut, run by the imd pathway, attacked the bacteria locally. Blood cells called hemocytes engulfed escapees in the body fluid. A systemic immune response appeared only when that engulfing was blocked.
europmc-pmc2126306: A medical paper studying paratyphoid bacilli isolated from hog-cholera cases. The pig germs. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2128106: A medical paper on roentgen ray intoxication, unit dose over thorax. The X-ray poisoning. This article preserves that radiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128206: A medical paper on the flagellum of the rat-bite fever microorganism. The germ's tail. This article preserves that bacteriology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128406: A medical paper on the reverse selective bacteriostatic action of acid fuchsin. The backwards dye. This article preserves that bacteriology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131206: A medical paper on influence of light on the growth and malignancy of a transplantable neoplasm. The lit tumors. This article preserves that oncology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140706: A biology paper on critical thermal increments for rhythmic respiratory movements of insects. The bugs' breathing heat. This article preserves that physiology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2244806:
Limb and Braun scanned the brains in 2008 of professional jazz pianists while they improvised. Spontaneous improvisation creates novel melody, harmony and rhythm on the spot, offering a window on creativity itself. The team used functional MRI with two tasks of very different complexity. Improvisation was compared against playing over-learned sequences from memory, isolating the brain pattern of spontaneous creation.

Improvisation consistently switched off large parts of the prefrontal cortex involved in self-monitoring and deliberate control. At the same time it focally activated the medial prefrontal cortex, a region tied to self-expression. Sensorimotor areas organising performance lit up widely. Limbic structures regulating emotion and motivation deactivated. The authors suggest this dissociated pattern, internally driven action without conscious self-censoring, provides the cognitive context letting spontaneous creativity emerge.
europmc-pmc2248206:
Kilbourne and co-workers applied the Replicating Effective Programs framework in 2007 to move proven health interventions into community settings. Effective programmes often stay trapped in the academic centres that created them. The framework comes from a United States disease control project that prepared HIV interventions for wide dissemination. It aims to preserve fidelity, delivering the programme as designed, while allowing local customisation for transfer to new settings.

The framework runs in four phases: pre-conditions, pre-implementation, implementation, and maintenance and evolution. Early phases identify need, target population and a suitable intervention. Later phases cover packaging, community input, training, technical assistance and evaluation. The authors argue the steps suit clinical and health services interventions generally. They call for strategies that keep the framework itself sustainable and for tests of those strategies.
europmc-pmc2268006:
Appel and co-workers showed in 2008 that one region of the hepatitis C virus protein NS5A is essential for assembling infectious particles. The virus chronically infects about three percent of the world's population and can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. NS5A binds viral RNA and was assumed to aid replication, but its role in particle production was unknown. The team deleted parts of NS5A in cell-based virus production systems and tracked particle formation.

The C-terminal domain III proved to be the primary determinant for assembly. Both the core protein and NS5A gather on the surface of lipid droplets, proposed assembly sites inside cells. Deleting domain III broke that co-location and abolished infectious particle formation. Core protein then piled up excessively on the droplets. Assembly defects could be rescued by supplying working NS5A separately, confirming the protein's direct role.
europmc-pmc2270306:
Mossong and co-workers surveyed social contacts in 2008 across eight European countries to ground infectious disease models. Models of respiratory infections often assumed mixing patterns with little evidence. In this study, 7,290 participants kept paper diaries for one day, recording 97,904 contacts with their age, sex, place, duration and whether physical. The aim was a common method across countries so results could be compared directly.

Mixing patterns proved remarkably similar across the eight countries. Contacts were strongly assortative by age, meaning people mix mostly with their own age group, especially schoolchildren and young adults. Long or daily contacts usually involved physical touch, while brief rare ones did not. Home, school and leisure contacts were more often physical than work or travel ones. Early modelling suggests five to nineteen-year-olds would suffer highest incidence first.
europmc-pmc2276506:
Ventura and Birch reviewed in 2008 whether parenting shapes children's eating and weight. Childhood obesity has risen dramatically worldwide, and school-based prevention has had limited success. The authors searched literature from October 2006 to January 2007 for studies linking parenting, child eating and child weight. Sixty-six articles met their criteria. Their aims were to judge causal evidence for parenting effects and to find promising parenting strategies for prevention programmes.

Most studies linked parenting to child eating rather than directly to weight. Experimental evidence showed parenting practices such as pressure to eat, restriction, modelling and food availability do influence children's eating. Evidence tying parenting to weight, or weight change through eating, was mostly cross-sectional, a single snapshot design that cannot prove direction. Few studies used proper mediation designs. The authors propose a multiphase optimisation approach for building better interventions.
europmc-pmc2287206:
Poldrack and co-authors issued guidelines in 2008 for reporting functional magnetic resonance imaging studies. Brain imaging papers are read by physicists, physiologists, psychologists and statisticians, each needing full methodological detail to judge or replicate the work. Missing details also starve large databases of the metadata needed for data mining and meta-analysis. The editorial sets out what every fMRI paper should specify, without dictating how studies must be done.

An appendix provides an explicit checklist authors can follow when preparing manuscripts. The guidelines are meant as a starting point for debate, not dogma. A wiki-based website was established so researchers can argue over and jointly edit them over time. The site also hosts an example methods section written to the guidelines. The authors want standards reflecting the whole field's current practice, not one group's opinion.
europmc-pmc2311306:
Sturm and co-authors introduced OpenMS in 2008, a free software framework for mass spectrometry. Mass spectrometry weighs molecules to identify what is in a sample. Labs use it heavily in proteomics, the study of all proteins in a cell, and in similar work on small molecules.

The problem they addressed was practical. New instruments produced ever larger data sets, yet existing tools were hard to combine or adapt. OpenMS offered shared building blocks, from basic data types to advanced methods for analysis, in one portable system. Other groups had already used it in published studies by 2008. It was released under an open licence, so any lab could use and extend it.
europmc-pmc2363506:
Yung and colleagues compared two oral drugs for a brain tumor that had come back in 2000. The tumor was glioblastoma multiforme, the most aggressive form of brain cancer. Patients whose cancer returned after first treatment have few options, and the trial tested temozolomide against an older drug, procarbazine.

The randomised study enrolled 225 patients at many centres. With temozolomide, 21% of patients reached six months without their cancer growing, versus 8% on procarbazine, a gap the trial judged significant. Median time before growth was 12.4 weeks on temozolomide and about 8.3 weeks on the older drug, and six-month survival was 60% versus 44% in the same comparison. Quality of life held up while the disease stayed controlled, whichever drug patients took. Side effects were mostly mild or moderate.
europmc-pmc2564806:
Chauhan and colleagues set out practical guidance in 2008 for how often glaucoma patients need visual field tests to catch worsening disease. Glaucoma slowly steals side vision, and the field test tracks the loss, but nobody had evidence-based rules for test frequency. The authors combined real variability data from patients with statistical modelling of how many tests detecting change requires.

Their tables show the tests per year needed to spot a given loss over two, three, or five years. For example, a patient with average test variability needs three examinations a year to confirm a 4-decibel drop in the summary score within two years. Slower loss or calmer test results need fewer visits, and noisier results need more. They also advise on test type, strategy, and quality checks.
europmc-pmc2671306:
Fair and colleagues charted in 2009 how children's brain networks grow into the adult pattern, shifting from local to spread out. The adult brain runs on specialized networks that cooperate flexibly. The team used resting brain scans, graph math, and community-finding tools to compare network layout in children and young adults.

Across four known networks, the same trend appeared. Links between nearby areas weakened with age, a process the authors call segregation. Chosen links between distant areas strengthened, an integration. As a result, children's network communities follow physical closeness, while adults' follow function. Both age groups still showed the efficient small-world layout, where any two areas connect through few steps. The authors argue this local-to-distributed shift is a general rule of brain development, with real effects on how thinking skills mature.
europmc-pmc2689706:
Singh, Rebbapragada, and Lykke-Andersen proposed in 2008 a unified answer to how human cells spot and destroy faulty gene messages. The system, nonsense-mediated decay, shreds messages with a premature stop signal, which would otherwise make broken proteins. Two rival theories had credited different sentries: a marker complex left by splicing, or a protein that sits on the message's tail.

The authors show the truth is a tug of war at the stop signal. The tail protein, PABP, when close, shields the message by blocking the decay crew's recruiter. The splicing marker, when present farther downstream, pulls the other way and boosts decay. Stretching the tail region beyond a threshold length triggered decay by itself. Many normal human messages have long tails yet survive, which the authors explain by stocking them with shielding factors near the stop.
europmc-pmc2691606:
Ueda and Wood traced in 2009 a hidden brake on biofilm building in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that plagues hospitals and cystic fibrosis lungs. They screened 5,850 mutant strains for odd film growth and found a standout: knocking out one gene, PA3885, multiplied biofilm 147-fold. The mutant clumped heavily, spread poorly, and secreted 28 times more matrix sugar than normal.

PA3885 makes an enzyme that drains a signal molecule called c-di-GMP. That signal tells bacteria to settle and build; the enzyme lowers it, keeping cells mobile. Without the brake, the signal soared and the film genes switched hard on. The cell's quorum sensing system, its population census, normally boosts the brake gene as crowds grow. The circuit thus links crowd counting to the settle-or-swim decision through one phosphatase enzyme.
europmc-pmc2700806:
Nugent and Jones presented in 2009 a machine-learning predictor for the layout of membrane proteins, a class that includes most drug targets. These proteins thread back and forth through the cell membrane, and knowing the threading pattern is a first step toward knowing function. Crystals of them are notoriously hard to grow, so they are scarce in structure databases despite their importance.

Their method, built on support vector machines, learns the pattern from the 131 membrane proteins whose structures are known. It predicts the full layout with 89 percent accuracy, and also calls the signal peptides that route proteins to the membrane, at 93 percent. A companion filter tells membrane proteins from ordinary soluble ones with almost no false alarms. Applied to whole genomes, the tools annotate a drug-rich protein family that experiments alone cannot keep up with.
europmc-pmc2717906:
Michie, Fixsen, Grimshaw, and Eccles warned in 2009 that complex behavior-change programs in health care are described too poorly to copy or judge. Such programs aim to change habits of patients or of the staff who treat them. Reviews of nearly a thousand studies found full detail in only a small share, and few teams checked if the program was delivered as planned.

Without clear terms for what was done, later teams cannot replicate success or learn which parts caused an effect. The authors call for a scientific method to specify and report each active part, dose, and delivery mode. Their journal, Implementation Science, would first encourage and then require such reporting from authors.
europmc-pmc2760206:
Ferree and Barbash showed in 2009 that species-specific heterochromatin, dense repetitive DNA around chromosome centers, can block chromosome segregation and kill hybrid offspring in fruit flies. Hybrid sterility and lethality are core parts of speciation, and known incompatibility genes were all protein-coding. Whether fast-evolving repetitive DNA itself could cause such isolation had never been clearly demonstrated.

In crosses between two Drosophila species, early embryos died from defects in segregating the paternal X chromosome during mitosis. The failure traced to a critical block of heterochromatic DNA carried on that X, whose sequence differs between species. A noncoding, repetitive region thus acts as a hybrid incompatibility factor, which widens the genetic basis of how new species split apart.
europmc-pmc2762806:
Fry and Neff reviewed in 2009 whether periodic prompts and reminders improve health promotion programs for weight loss, physical activity, and diet. Phones and the Internet now let programs send regular messages cheaply, but no comprehensive review had tested if such limited-contact prompting works or which features matter most. They searched studies from early 2008 that used ongoing prompts with a behavioral or biological outcome.

Nineteen studies with over fifteen thousand participants met their criteria, and eleven reported positive findings for periodic prompts. Effects looked stronger when prompts were frequent and when a counselor added personal contact. Long-term change could not be judged, since follow-up was short in most studies. They urge rigorous trials that vary prompt frequency and type to find what sustains change.
europmc-pmc2776306:
Nativio and co-authors showed in 2009 that cohesin is required for the folded shape of chromatin at the imprinted IGF2-H19 locus. Cohesin is a protein complex best known for holding sister DNA copies together. At this locus, the CTCF protein organizes parent-specific folding and blocks enhancers from the wrong gene. Cohesin sits with CTCF at many sites, but whether it builds the folds was unknown.

They used chromosome conformation capture, which maps which DNA stretches touch. They also depleted cohesin in human cells. Without cohesin, the locus lost its CTCF-mediated folding. IGF2 expression changed as the folding broke down. The folded state existed in both main phases of the cell cycle, so it does not depend on cohesin's sister-holding job. They propose that cohesin loops DNA within one chromosome to insulate genes. It does this much as it links sister copies.
europmc-pmc2868906:
Qin and colleagues ran a head-to-head contest in 2010 among the gene switches labs use to force cells to make chosen proteins. Eight always-on switches, called constitutive promoters, came from viruses and housekeeping genes of mammals and fruit flies. A ninth switch stays off until the drug doxycycline turns it on, which gives researchers timing control.

Across many cell types from several species, the always-on switches differed widely in strength, though most kept a similar rank from cell to cell. One virus-derived switch varied sharply between cell types, a trap for the unwary. At full induction the drug-controlled switch matched a strong always-on switch, so timing control costs little power. The rankings help researchers pick the right switch for each experiment.
europmc-pmc2874506:
Simera and colleagues argued in 2010 that health research is wasted when reports leave out key details, and they presented the EQUATOR Network as the fix. Electronic publishing makes full reporting easier than ever, yet reports still routinely omit how studies were designed and run. The network is an international effort to raise reporting quality across health research.

EQUATOR maintains a free online library of reporting guidelines, the checklists that tell authors what a complete report must include for each study type. It also runs training and helps groups draft new guidelines where none exist. The authors urge journals, funders, and universities to require the checklists, since clear reports are what let readers judge, reuse, and build on a study's results.
europmc-pmc2874806:
Schellenberger, Park, Conrad, and Palsson launched in 2010 BiGG, a shared knowledge base of computer models of cell metabolism. Such models rebuild an organism's full chemical reaction network from its genome and predict what the cell can make and burn. As models multiplied, each lab used its own naming, which blocked comparison across organisms.

BiGG merges published models into one resource with standard names for genes, proteins, reactions, and chemicals. Visitors can browse model contents, view pathway maps, and download models in a standard file format for their own software. Links lead outward to gene and chemical databases for deeper detail. Freely available for academic use, the base gave the systems biology field a common, curated starting point.
europmc-pmc2918506:
Burd and colleagues challenged in 2010 the dogma that heavy weights are required to build muscle, testing young men's muscle protein synthesis after leg training at different loads. Fifteen men performed knee extensions three ways: heavy load to failure, light load matched in work to the heavy session, and light load taken all the way to failure. Tracer infusion and biopsies measured new protein built in the hours and day after each session.

Light-to-failure training matched heavy training for contractile protein synthesis at four hours. It was also the only mode still running far above rest a full day later. At that point it sat at about double the resting rate. Light work stopped short of failure lagged behind both. Reaching failure with light loads recruits the full muscle and sustains the building signal, a finding with rehab and aging implications.
europmc-pmc2929606:
Basu and Krishnamurthy reviewed how cells respond to DNA damage caused by cisplatin, a widely used cancer drug, in a 2010 article. Cisplatin kills tumour cells mainly by harming their DNA, yet some cancers resist it.

Their account follows the drug from entry into the cell through repair attempts, detox routes, and signals that push the cell toward death. Protein kinases help govern that death programme, called apoptosis, after damage is sensed. Knowing which pathways control sensitivity could guide better drug pairings and help doctors predict which tumours will respond to cisplatin treatment.
europmc-pmc3012106:
Schäfer and colleagues mined insurance claims from about a hundred and fifty thousand Germans past sixty-five to find patterns among chronic diseases in a 2010 study. Carrying several conditions at once raises death and disability, yet which diseases travel together was murky.

Statistical factoring of forty-six diagnosis groups yielded three patterns in each sex. One cluster joined heart and metabolic disorders. A second mixed anxiety, depression, unexplained symptoms, and pain. A third grouped brain and psychiatric disorders. The heart-metabolic pattern covered about a third of women and more of men. Knowing the clusters can sharpen diagnosis, prevention, and care planning.
europmc-pmc3019106:
Schijman led an international study in 2011 comparing laboratory DNA tests for Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, across expert labs in sixteen countries. A century after discovery, diagnosis and judging cure after treatment still needed dependable tools.

Panels included pure parasite DNA dilutions, blood spiked with parasite cells, and samples from dozens of patients with known status. Dozens of test variants targeted three parasite DNA regions. Commercial kits and satellite DNA tests proved most specific, while another target caught the faintest traces of one parasite type. Performance gaps argue for shared standards before results can guide treatment.
europmc-pmc3029306:
Sobhani and a French team compared in 2011 the gut bacteria of people with colon cancer and people with healthy colons. Gut microbe balance is tied to general health, and the team wanted to know whether cancer comes with a distinct imbalance. Stool from close to one hundred eighty patients was tested before their colon exams, using gene sequencing and targeted counts.

Overall bacteria counts were similar in both groups, yet the mix differed. One large group, Bacteroides and Prevotella together, ran higher in cancer patients. Immune cells that make a signal called IL17 were also more common in the healthy looking tissue of cancer patients. The authors call this the first large study of its kind. They suggest the shifts could inform future screening and studies of how microbes interact with the gut lining.
europmc-pmc3091306:
Herzog and colleagues introduced in 2011 a query language and software kit for identifying fats in shotgun mass spectrometry, where a whole lipid extract is sprayed directly into the instrument. A cell's full set of lipids can hold tens of thousands of distinct molecules, and reading their fragmentation patterns by hand is the field's bottleneck. Their system, LipidXplorer, lets users write rules describing how each lipid class breaks apart.

The software then matches those rules against spectra from any instrument brand and reports how much of each individual lipid species is present. Because the rules are written by users rather than hard coded, new lipid classes can be added without new software. The kit is open source. The authors present it as a general solution for accurate lipid counting across labs and machines, a step toward comparing lipid profiles between studies.
europmc-pmc3111406:
Rym Boulkedid and colleagues published a 2011 review in PLoS ONE on how expert panels pick quality measures for health care. The method they study asks experts in rounds, sharing group feedback until agreement forms. Their team searched three decades of studies that used this approach to choose care indicators.

Among eighty studies, basic reporting varied widely, and many papers left out response rates, feedback steps, or how agreement was reached. Most panels mixed different kinds of stakeholders, with a median size in the high teens, and validity was the most used test of a good measure. The authors offer practical guidance so future panels report their work fully enough for others to trust and repeat.
europmc-pmc3143906:
Stefano Schiaffino and Cristina Mammucari reviewed the main growth pathway in skeletal muscle in a 2011 paper in Skeletal Muscle. A hormone signal, passed down a chain of cell switches, tells muscle fibres to build protein and holds back protein breakdown. Evidence from engineered mice and muscle transfer experiments anchors the review.

The central switch balances two arms: one driving the protein-building machinery, the other restraining a family of factors that switch on disposal genes. The pathway proves vital for muscle growth during development and repair after injury. Its role when adult muscle answers heavy loading, though, is far less certain. Knowing the wiring exactly could guide drugs against wasting from disease and aging.
europmc-pmc3210606:
Juan Peng and colleagues reviewed fucoxanthin, a pigment from brown seaweeds and diatoms, in this 2011 article in Marine Drugs. The compound colors brown algae and has drawn attention for possible health benefits. The authors summarize the scientific literature on how the body handles fucoxanthin and what effects it may have.

Reported activities include antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, anti-obesity, and antidiabetic effects, along with protection for the liver, brain blood vessels, bones, skin, and eyes. One problem is absorption: the human body takes up little fucoxanthin from seaweed on its own. Eating it with oil or fat appears to improve uptake, which the authors say could make it a promising marine-derived drug candidate.
europmc-pmc3219706:
Bianli Xu and colleagues hunted the cause of a mysterious illness in Henan Province, China, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Since 2007, patients had developed fever with low platelet and white cell counts, often after tick bites. Tests explained only a small share of cases, so the team screened patient blood with an unbiased metagenomic method that reads all genetic material present.

The screen found a previously unknown bunyavirus, present only in patients' samples. Follow-up testing found viral RNA in most acute-phase samples, and antibody studies confirmed recent infection in most patients with paired samples. The virus was grown in culture and named Henan Fever Virus; its genome proved nearly identical to a virus reported elsewhere as SFTSV. The evidence ties the new virus strongly to the syndrome.
europmc-pmc3230406:
Georg Matt and a large team laid out the case for studying thirdhand smoke in this 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Thirdhand smoke is the residue tobacco smoke leaves behind on surfaces, in dust, and in air long after a cigarette is out. Its health impact was far less understood than that of secondhand smoke, and the authors argue the ambiguity needs resolving.

They define the terms and review what was known. Residue persists in real homes and transforms over time into secondary pollutants that can be more toxic. It leaves nicotine on hands. It also leaves smoke markers in the urine of nonsmokers living where smokers once lived. Much remains unknown about its chemistry, exposure routes, and health effects. The paper proposes a coordinated, multidisciplinary research agenda to close those gaps.
europmc-pmc3261106:
Juan-Manuel Belda-Lois and colleagues reviewed rehabilitation of walking after stroke in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine. They examine classical therapy techniques alongside newer technology, asking what happens when treatment is organized top-down, driven by the brain's ability to rewire itself. The methods surveyed include hands-on physiotherapy approaches, electrical stimulation of muscles, robotic devices, and brain-computer interfaces.

No single classical approach proved clearly better than the others, though combining strategies beat walking practice alone. Electrical stimulation paired with gait retraining improved stroke patients' walking. Robots still need research proving their value for over-ground walking. Brain-computer interface work has concentrated on arms, though hints suggest shared mechanisms may aid both arm and leg recovery. The authors look ahead to brain imaging that could tailor treatment to each patient.
europmc-pmc3373106:
Budke, Deplazes, and Torgerson set out in 2006 to price the worldwide burden of cystic echinococcosis, a tapeworm disease. People and livestock pick up the parasite's eggs, and cysts then grow in the liver, lungs, or other organs. Dogs carry the adult worm, and farm animals carry the cyst stage.

No global tally of the disease's health and money costs existed, so the authors combined lost healthy years with financial losses. Costs include treatment, lost wages, and livestock production losses. The disease is preventable, yet it is spreading in places such as the former Soviet Union and parts of China. Their estimate gives control programs a basis for claiming scarce funding.
europmc-pmc3397506:
Xu and colleagues built computer models in 2012 to predict how much of a swallowed drug actually reaches the body, its oral bioavailability. Two gatekeepers, a pump protein and liver enzyme family, block many drugs at this step. Their models were the first to build those gatekeepers in from the start, using over eight hundred varied drug-like molecules.

Three modeling styles were compared and checked by cross-validation and outside test sets. The nonlinear support-vector method edged out the two linear ones in accuracy. All three, though, showed real promise for screening candidates early. Such models can spare the slow, costly lab testing that new drug design usually requires.
europmc-pmc3419206:
Martínez-González and the PREDIMED investigators tested in 2012 whether a short fourteen-question diet tool could capture the link between Mediterranean eating and slimmer bodies. Full diet surveys are costly and slow, while a brief tool can give instant feedback in trials. Their test bed was the full PREDIMED trial group: over seven thousand older adults at high heart risk.

Higher scores on the short tool tracked strongly with lower body mass, waist size, and waist-to-height ratio, matching the full survey's verdict. People scoring at the top had notably lower odds of a risky waist-to-height ratio than low scorers. Eating plenty of nuts and going easy on sweetened drinks drove the strongest links. A two-minute questionnaire, they show, can carry real weight.
europmc-pmc3458106:
Pettersson and colleagues found in 2012 that female mice shrug off the metabolic harm of a high-fat diet that sickens males. Sex gaps in obesity complications such as type 2 diabetes are well reported, but the mechanism was open. For fourteen weeks mice ate control or fatty food while weight, blood sugar, and insulin were tracked, followed by deep immune and pancreas checks.

Females gained as much weight as males yet kept normal insulin and glucose tolerance, while males became insulin-loaded and intolerant. Obese females showed no body-wide inflammation, and their belly fat grew richer in calming regulatory T cells. Males went the other way: inflamed fat, fewer regulatory cells, and swollen insulin-making islets. The immune setting inside fat, they argue, decides the outcome.
europmc-pmc3458906:
Cohen and colleagues systematically reviewed malaria resurgences in 2012, the comebacks that have haunted control programs for a century. Funding since 2000 had driven malaria down, but history warns that gains melt when vigilance does. The team hunted the literature for documented resurgence events and sorted every proposed cause into three baskets.

They found seventy-five events across sixty-one countries, spanning the nineteen thirties to the two thousands. Nearly all involved, at least in part, a weakening of the control program, and money trouble was the single most common reason. Rising transmission potential played a role in over half, while drug or insecticide resistance explained a minority. Keeping today's programs funded and running, they urge, is the main lesson of the past.
