The review will gather studies of refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced youth aged ten to nineteen. It will span qualitative, quantitative, and mixed designs, where the intervention aims at psychological well-being or social functioning. The finished map is meant to steer policy and practice toward the gaps, showing which groups and which kinds of help researchers have ignored.
plos-pone-0349606:
Lotte J S Fleurkens-Ewals and co-authors ran a reader study in 2026 on scoring cancer spread inside the abdomen from CT scans. The score guides treatment for cancers that seed the belly lining, and pre-drawn region outlines might help readers agree.

Eighty-two clinicians from nineteen countries scored nine scans, with and without colour overlays marking the regions. Agreement, closeness to the surgical score, confidence, and user experience were compared. The overlays did not significantly improve agreement, the headline the authors report plainly. Negative results like this save hospitals from buying decision aids that feel helpful but do not measurably help.
plos-pone-0350006:
Karina Patasova, Marie Holmqvist, and co-authors hunted for hidden genetic links between systemic sclerosis, a rare autoimmune disease, and the cancers its patients develop at elevated rates. Whole-genome comparisons had found no overall relationship, but averaging can hide local links where effects point in opposite directions. Their 2026 study applied finer methods that test genetic correlation region by region against breast and lung cancers and blood malignancies.

Again, no overall genetic correlation appeared. Zooming in, though, they found twenty-three local regions where the diseases' genetics correlated significantly, some positively and some negatively, exactly the pattern global methods miss. Follow-up analyses probed genes in those regions for shared biology. The authors argue the sclerosis-cancer connection may live in specific genomic neighborhoods rather than across the whole genome.
plos-pone-0350106:
Hye Young Hong and Young Ae Kang led a review of lung patients in Korea. The illness is a slow lung infection from a germ kin to the TB germ. Care takes a year or more of drugs. Many patients quit too soon. The team followed four hundred twenty patients treated from 2010 to 2023. They split those who quit early from those who finished.

Thirty in a hundred quit early. Bad drug side effects raised the odds of quitting a lot. Poor diet did too. Quitters then died at near three times the rate of finishers. Low diet scores also tracked with death. The team urges close watch for side effects and food support from day one.
plos-pone-0350506:
Donrawee Waeyeng and Soisungwan Satarug led a study of diet and kidney health in southern Thailand. People there face long-term contact with two toxic metals, cadmium and lead. Both metals can harm the kidneys. The team asked if eating more plant foods might help. They signed up ninety-six adults aged fifty and over in late 2024.

People who ate more plant foods showed less of a urine sign of kidney cell harm. Those who ate more nuts and seeds did best of all. High metal contact, by contrast, came with signs of kidney stress. The team says plant-rich diets may soften metal harm. They also back the urine test as an early warning tool.
plos-pone-0350806:
Felix A Andong and colleagues studied breeding male village weaver birds in Amurum Forest Reserve, Nigeria, during the costly season when males breed, moult, and fight infection at once. One hundred and forty eight males were grouped by worm infection and moult status. Blood stress balance, blood sugar, and feather colour quality were measured within minutes of capture.

About half the males carried the worms. Infected birds showed strained stress chemistry. Males facing both infection and moult scored worst on sugar control and feather quality by far, beyond either burden alone in direct contrasts. Bright honest signals, the work shows, collapse first when body budgets are doubly drained.
plos-pone-0351106:
Akram Hasanov and four colleagues study the wildest days in energy stock markets — the rare crashes and spikes that standard risk models handle badly, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Using two decades of daily data to early 2025, they estimated how quickly the chance of extreme returns decays for renewable and conventional energy share indices. The method asks, in effect, how many statistical moments of the return distribution even exist.

Both kinds of index showed heavy tails following a power law. Average returns and volatility appear finite and usable, but higher shape measures may be mathematically infinite, which quietly breaks tools built on them. A rolling analysis showed tail risk swelling around major market stresses. Investors in green energy, the authors warn, should plan for extremes that history understates.
plos-pone-0351306:
Markku Kallio and colleagues pooled data on close to sixteen hundred children with confirmed bacterial meningitis in six countries across Latin America, Angola, and Finland. Simple spinal fluid tests at admission, sugar, protein, and white cell counts, were checked against death in hospital and brain outcome at discharge. Such cheap tests could help triage where intensive care is scarce.

Death rose step by step as spinal fluid sugar fell and as protein rose. Children with both very low sugar and very high protein died at a rate near twenty seven percent, versus one percent when both values looked normal. Low white cell counts also warned of danger. Two routine numbers together, the authors show, flag high risk children early.
plos-pone-0351406:
Bian and colleagues audited urine leakage prevention for intensive care patients with catheters in a Chinese hospital in a 2026 study. The team first built audit standards from the best available evidence, then checked real practice with dozens of nurses and patients. Gaps between standards and bedside care were then analyzed for causes.

Audits of this kind sort which failures come from knowledge, staffing, supplies, or habit. That sorting shapes training and workflow fixes in the next phase of the project. Catheter leakage harms skin, comfort, and infection risk, so even small compliance gains matter in units where patients stay for weeks. The baseline review gives the unit a clear starting measure.
plos-pone-0351506:
Long COVID symptoms vary wildly between people, so Su-jin Kim and Jinhee Kim sorted Korean adults with lasting symptoms into natural groups. Their 2026 PLOS One survey covered about six hundred thirty adults whose symptoms had run at least twelve weeks, scoring twenty-six complaints and overall quality of life.

Four profiles fit best. About a quarter had light symptoms overall; the largest group, over two fifths, had moderate problems across many body systems; another group centered on exhaustion that worsens after effort. Quality of life fell as symptom load rose. The authors say clinics should treat these profiles differently rather than handing everyone the same plan.
plos-pone-0351606:
Editorial Note: PLOS One flags an overlap concern between a published study of DNA sequences in ice from Antarctica's subglacial Lake Vostok and a companion paper by the same group. This 2026 note explains that both articles analyze the same two ice cores, which the authors had declared before publication.

The authors say the papers differ in focus: one on the lake's likely living conditions, the other on which species and body processes the sequences suggest. An independent editorial board member reviewed the overlap question. Readers should keep the shared dataset in mind when weighing the two papers' conclusions about life beneath the Antarctic ice.
plos-pone-0351706:
Dinh Thi Nguyen and Loan Thi Ho catalogued the leaf beetles of Cat Ba Island, a limestone island off northern Vietnam, pairing old-fashioned specimen work with DNA barcoding. Shelf islands in Southeast Asia are biological crossroads and among the least surveyed places for insects. Field collecting found thirty-six species-level units across thirty genera, dominated by one large subfamily.

Barcoding sorted the catch into thirty-one genetic clusters, most of them new to the global barcode library, proof of how much diversity sits undocumented on one island. Clock estimates place the main lineages' origins in the Miocene, before the island itself took shape, so the beetles are heirs of mainland forests later stranded by rising seas. For conservation, Cat Ba is not a depauperate offshoot but an archive, and its beetles deserve the archive's protection.
plos-pone-0352206:
Lismaryin Muñoz-Requene, Pedro Sánchez-Zamora, and Rosa Gallardo-Cobos measured how exposed Nicaragua's North Caribbean Coast is to tropical cyclones, town by town. The region is among the country's most storm-hit and poorest, and climate change is loading the dice further. They built a vulnerability index from twelve indicators covering exposure, the fragility of people and housing, and each municipality's capacity to adapt.

The map that emerged is uneven. Bonanza combined high exposure and fragility with weak adaptive capacity, while Waslala showed sturdier structure. Three clusters of towns shared similar risk profiles. A single regional plan would fit none of them well. For disaster agencies, the index names where shelters, drainage, and income support buy the most safety before the next storm season, not after the damage is photographed.
plos-pone-0352506:
Isabel von Känel-Cordoba and seven colleagues gather everything known about the half-distance Ironman triathlon, in this 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review. The event — a swim, a long bike ride, and a half marathon — has boomed worldwide, yet research has trailed the full-distance race. Searching five databases, the team assembled eighty-six studies covering training, nutrition, body measures, weather, and medical issues.

Cycling emerged as the strongest single predictor of finish time. Professional men peaked around age twenty-eight, women around thirty-two, and participation is growing fastest among women and older athletes. Racing temporarily dents immunity and muscles, then recovers. The authors note the field's blind spots: small samples and too few women studied.
plos-pone-0352906:
Rafael Flores and co-authors designed a family of lipoic-acid-derived molecules aimed at a brain receptor tied to neurodegeneration. The sigma-1 receptor is implicated in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, and diverse, easy-to-make activators are wanted. Their 2026 design follows a three-part recipe: a sulphur-bearing hydrophobic head, a flexible amide linker, and a greasy tail.

Twenty-one molecules were designed, docked in the computer, synthesised, and tested for binding at both sigma receptor types. Three stood out for selective sigma-1 binding in the nanomolar range, though a standard comparison ligand bound far tighter still. Flores and colleagues keep the three as starting leads for a follow-up round of structure tuning.
plos-pone-0353106:
Yinchun Wang and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One language study of Chinese scholars speaking academic English. Their focus is hedging, the words speakers use to soften claims. Hedging is a known stumbling block at conferences and defenses. The team built a large corpus of Chinese scholars' spoken English. They compared it with an American academic speech corpus. Verb-based hedges were the focus.

Chinese scholars used far fewer personal stance markers like 'I think.' They used far more shared markers like 'we see.' The authors read this as a strategy that favors group harmony and shared duty. The study does not stop at diagnosis. It builds a classroom module with worksheets to train these forms. The aim is fewer communication failures in high-stakes settings.
plos-pone-0353206:
Limin Tang and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on licorice stem and leaf silage as cattle feed, tested in laboratory rumen fluid rather than live animals. The team prepared silage at four dry matter levels and followed fermentation over seventy-two hours, measuring gas output, acidity, nutrient breakdown, and the microbes involved. A licorice feed additive was included in the silage.

The batch at fifty-five percent dry matter performed best overall, producing the most gas and microbial protein, breaking down nutrients fastest, and supporting the richest microbial community. Helpful fermentation products also peaked earlier in that batch. Statistical rankings placed it first among the four, and the authors recommend that moisture level for turning licorice stems and leaves into useful dairy feed.
plos-pone-0353306:
Wieland and colleagues compared two advanced methods for fitting random epidemic models in a 2026 study. Epidemic models that include chance events help forecast outbreaks, but working out their settings from data is mathematically hard. The team tested both methods on three standard disease models of rising complexity.

Each method had to recover known settings from data produced by the models themselves. Their strengths differed by model and data richness, giving modelers a practical guide on which to pick. Fast, reliable fitting matters during real outbreaks, when officials need quick forecasts that honestly reflect uncertainty. The comparison saves future teams from choosing a fitting tool blind.
plos-pone-0353506:
Sabah and Alaa presented a self-tuning method for grouping texts by topic in a 2026 study. Modern language models turn text into rich numeric codes, but each model shines in different fields. Older blending methods fix how much each model counts ahead of time, wasting their complementary strengths.

Their framework lets a search algorithm adjust the blend weights as grouping proceeds, with no labels needed. Better blends should give cleaner clusters for tasks like news sorting and routing technical questions. The work targets a quiet but costly step in text systems, where poor grouping early on degrades every later answer. Dynamic weighting offers a path to clusters that fit each collection's own character.
plos-pone-0353606:
Hattan Abutarboush and colleagues report in 2026 on a thin microwave absorber built from printed rings. Their design uses two nested rings on a common circuit board material, with four small stubs placed evenly around the outer ring and a solid metal backing. Keeping the build to one layer was the central aim.

Tests of a made sample matched computer models and showed strong uptake in six separate frequency bands, each above nine tenths of the incoming energy. Lower bands linked mainly to magnetic responses, while higher bands mixed electric effects as well. A simple flat design that handles several bands at once could help with shielding, sensing, and reducing unwanted radar reflections.
plos-pone-0353706:
Natthapon Inta, Annmarie Grealish, and Mary Leamy explore what recovery from mental illness means in Thailand, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. Recovery is a guiding idea in modern mental health care, but its meaning shifts between cultures. They spoke with service users, family carers, and health professionals in primary and community services, then tested the themes in feedback workshops.

Participants described recovery as moving from symptom relief toward hope, meaning, and social connection. Family backing, community acceptance, and trusting relationships with staff were central, while obstacles appeared at personal, family, service, and community levels. From this, the authors propose a recovery support model fitted to Thai culture.
plos-pone-0353906:
Niu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether immune system genes raise the risk of clogged heart arteries in people from Northeast China. The HLA genes help the immune system tell self from invader, and they vary a lot between people. The team compared two HLA genes in about two hundred people, split between those prone to artery clogging and controls.

Dozens of gene variants were counted. Two single variants appeared more often in the disease-prone group, but neither survived strict correction for the many tests run. A paired combination of the two variants, inherited together, was more than twice as common in the disease-prone group. That signal also faded under the strictest correction, though its size was too large, the authors argue, to dismiss as pure noise. They label the pair a candidate risk marker and call for much larger studies to confirm or refute it.
plos-pone-0354206:
Lyu and colleagues, in a 2026 review, work out how much exercise helps depression among middle-aged and older people with Parkinson's disease, and which kinds help most. Earlier trials tested exercise one dose at a time, which hid the shape of the benefit. The team pooled twenty-five trials and modeled dose on a continuous scale, counting weekly energy spent.

Benefit followed a curve, not a straight climb. Gains held across a broad middle band of weekly dose and peaked near its center; at the highest doses the effect turned unstable. Two kinds of exercise stood out: exercise paired with mental training, and mind-body exercise such as tai chi styles, both peaking at the same middle dose. Walking helped only at higher doses, and several other types showed no dependable range. The authors say dose and kind must be prescribed together, like a drug and its amount.
plos-pone-0354606:
Nnaemeka Iriemenam and co-authors tested front-line health staff at seven Nigerian sites for coronavirus antibodies late in the pandemic. Health staff faced the worst exposure, and counts of past infection guide safety plans. Their 2026 study enrolled more than twelve hundred nurses, lab staff, doctors, and pharmacists for blood tests and a habits survey.

Antibodies were near universal: about ninety-eight in one hundred staff tested as past-exposed. Most hits bore the mark of the virus's inner protein, a sign of true past infection, not shots alone. Nurses were three times as apt to test as past-exposed as lab staff. Half the staff still lacked shots at the time. The team urges stronger shots and ward safety for front-line staff.
plos-pone-0354706:
Fei Chen and co-authors propose in 2026 a better way to estimate the health of lithium ion batteries from electrical response tests. Single response measures miss how ageing parts of a battery interact, giving weak predictions. Their method picks several response features that track capacity loss, then feeds them to a neural network tuned by three search methods borrowed from nature.

Across test conditions with plenty of data and with noisy, scarce data, tuned networks kept errors low and stable. Two of the tuning methods stood out in the hardest cases. Reliable health estimates matter for safe use of batteries in vehicles and portable devices.
plos-pone-0355106:
Issiaka Sare and co-authors tested a locally isolated fungus as a malaria mosquito killer and traced its effects across generations. Fungi offer an eco-friendlier alternative to chemical insecticides, but their full life-history costs to mosquitoes were unclear. Their 2026 study exposed a major malaria vector to two strains of the fungus at larval and adult stages.

Larvae were reared in spore-dosed water, and survivors were followed for lifespan, wing size, egg laying, and blood feeding. Separately, sprayed adult females were followed through their offspring's survival. Survival analysis used standard hazard models, with other traits compared across treatments. Sare and colleagues frame the results for biocontrol planners weighing fungal sprays against resistance-prone chemicals.
plos-pone-0355406:
Amit Hasan and co-authors report in 2026 the first known case in Bangladesh of a fungus causing leaf spot on quinoa, a nutritious grain like crop with growing local promise. Sick plants at a university farm in Dhaka yielded one fungus again and again from spotted leaves. Shape study, gene sequencing, and family tree analysis named the culprit, and infection tests on healthy plants reproduced the spots.

The fungus was reisolated from the newly sick plants, completing the classic proof of cause. Colonies grew grey to black with curved, thick walled spores. The authors warn growers to watch for this emerging threat and urge resistance screening and joined up disease control.
plos-pone-0355506:
Benedicto Mgala and colleagues explore in 2026 daily life for patients in Tanzania who must take warfarin for life after receiving an artificial heart valve. The drug prevents dangerous clots but needs tight dose control, a strict diet, and regular blood checks. Twelve patients at the national heart institute gave in depth interviews about their routines.

Many felt better after surgery, yet diet limits, side effects, low mood, and lost work weighed heavily. Keeping blood levels in range was hard amid money strain, uneven drug use, mixed advice, and scarce testing away from the centre. The authors call for a clearer, joined up path of care.
plos-pone-0355606: Cervical cancers resist immunotherapy through epigenetic trickery involving HDAC2. This paper showed HDAC2 restrains IGF2BP1-associated m6A dysregulation driving that resistance. The mechanistic chain reveals a druggable target that could re-sensitize tumors to immune attack.
plos-pone-0356006:
Vicente Lopez-Chavarrias, Irene Aldea, and Jovita Fernández-Pinero published a 2026 software paper in PLOS ONE introducing PePApipe, a tool that automates genome analysis for African swine fever virus. The virus devastates pig farming and triggers trade bans, and tracing outbreaks needs full genomes, yet the analysis steps were scattered across separate programs. The pipeline chains thirteen tools into one workflow, from raw sequencing reads through quality checks, genome assembly, and variant listing.

PePApipe was built for laboratory professionals with little computing background, needing only basic command-line skills, and it can run on a single machine or a computing cluster for batches. Outputs arrive in structured folders: a consensus genome plus a file of differences from a chosen reference, with intermediate files kept and steps switchable. The authors say one automated path cuts user error and makes results reproducible, easing the step from sequencer to outbreak report.
plos-pone-0356206:
Daisuke Sudo and Daisuke Toyoda ran a pilot trial testing whether eye exercise training adds anything to leg strengthening for thirty community-dwelling older adults. The bid was to cut falls by sharpening vision. Their 2026 randomized study trained both groups' legs for eight weeks. Half also drilled six visual skills on a dedicated training system. The skills ran from eye-hand coordination to peripheral perception.

No clear advantage appeared. Adjusted comparisons showed no confirmed differences in visual or physical outcomes. Several estimates leaned toward the vision group on exactly the skills practiced, though with wide uncertainty. The authors are candid: thirty people cannot settle the question. The pilot's real product is a blueprint for a properly powered trial with fairer controls and meaningful endpoints.
plos-pone-0356806:
Irina Elena Ionescu and colleagues compared two standard recipes for growing dendritic cells, the immune system's teaching cells, from mouse bone marrow, because the recipe quietly changes what the cells become. Their 2026 laboratory study grew cells with one growth factor alone or with a second added, then compared surface markers, cytokine output, and the ability to coach naive T cells.

Cells grown with the single factor looked mature yet still answered bacterial stimuli with cytokines and primed T cells in an antigen-specific way. Adding the second factor kept cells less mature but introduced nonspecific T cell signaling that could muddy experiments. The message for immunologists is to choose, and re-check, the recipe against the exact question being asked.
plos-pone-0356906:
Guillaume Bouguéon and colleagues test how long prepared bags of idarubicin, a workhorse drug against blood cancers, stay safe to use. Hospital pharmacies would like to prepare doses ahead, but shelf life in modern plastic bags lacked solid data. The team filled bags at two strengths in two common fluids. Some bags were stored cold. Others sat at room temperature. Samples were assayed across a full month, alongside checks for particles, acidity, and salt balance.

Drug levels stayed above ninety-five percent of the starting strength through day thirty in every condition, with no breakdown products detected. Bags showed no color change or precipitate, particle counts stayed within limits, and acidity and salt balance did not drift. Bouguéon and colleagues say pharmacies can safely prepare a month ahead under either storage style.
plos-pone-0357006:
Nayana Gunathilaka, Deshaka Jayakody, and Iranga Dilshan mapped fifteen years of rickettsioses in Sri Lanka. These are tick- and mite-borne fevers that are often missed. Their 2026 analysis used weekly national case reports from all twenty-five districts between 2009 and 2023. Satellite weather data was paired with the reports. The aim was to find where and when the diseases strike, and which climate conditions travel with them.

More than eighteen thousand cases were reported. They were heavily concentrated in Jaffna in the north, with the central highlands next. The modeling linked incidence patterns to local climate and geography. Knowing the hotspots and seasons lets health officials aim fever testing, public warnings, and vector control. They can target the districts and months where these under-recognized illnesses actually cluster.
plos-pone-0357106:
Julia Ruß and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in veterinary medicine. It measures serum reverse triiodothyronine, a thyroid-related hormone in blood, in three groups of dogs: those with hypothyroidism, those whose illness is not thyroidal, and healthy dogs. Thyroid tests in dogs are notoriously muddied by other illnesses.

Nonthyroidal illness can make a healthy thyroid look underactive, leading to wrong treatment. Comparing this hormone across the three groups tests whether it separates true thyroid failure from the shadow of other disease. Veterinarians diagnosing sluggish, gaining dogs are the readers who need cleaner thyroid markers.
plos-pone-0357206:
Ruy Felipe Melo Viegas led a team of eight authors who compared blood and saliva tests in heart failure patients, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Checking a failing heart now means drawing blood to measure stress and injury markers. The team asked whether saliva could carry the same signals in useful amounts.

Viegas and his co-authors measured three markers in both fluids: one linked to heart strain, one to heart muscle injury, and one to inflammation. Setting the saliva values beside the blood values shows how close a spit test could come to the standard. A simple saliva check would make repeat testing easier for patients who need close tracking.
plos-pone-0357406:
Huawei Wang led a team of five authors improving crane scheduling in railway freight yards, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rail-mounted gantry cranes move containers between trains and trucks, and poor scheduling jams the whole yard. The team built a flexible scheduling method that balances several goals at once.

Wang's model weighs speed against energy use and fairness across jobs, instead of chasing one target. Yards must make that trade-off daily as trains arrive off schedule. A model that bends without breaking helps dispatchers keep freight moving. Faster, steadier yards lower the cost of rail freight, which matters for shifting goods off roads and cutting transport emissions at the same time.
plos-pone-0357706:
Aysegul Erinc and colleagues ask whether a simple blood score predicts survival in people with scarring lung disease who do not have diabetes. The score combines fasting sugar and blood fat values and is often read as a sign of insulin resistance. Records covered well over a hundred patients on anti-scarring therapy, followed for close to three years on median, with lung tests and survival tracked.

The abstract reports the cohort's profile and the study design in detail, linking the score with lung function and death from any cause. Because patients here stayed within the non-diabetic range, the work tests whether small shifts in the score still carry meaning. Erinc and colleagues frame the score as a cheap add-on to scans and lung tests when judging outlook.
plos-pone-0357806:
Katie L Kowalski led a team of eight authors measuring rehabilitation science across Canada, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked who produces rehabilitation research, how much they publish, and what impact it has. Their data mixed public records with a survey of faculty across the country.

Kowalski's faculty-wide picture shows where the field is strong, where it is thin, and who shapes its future. Universities and funders can use that picture to spot gaps, such as regions or topics with few active researchers. Rehabilitation serves an aging population with growing needs, so the health of its research base matters beyond academia. The study offers a baseline for judging future growth.
plos-pone-0357906:
J. Richard T. Korecki and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for project FIERCE, a trial testing a meditation program built for stressed doctors. Most healthcare providers report burnout, poor sleep, and low mood from workplace strain, and mindfulness courses help but rarely target positive emotion. Their six-week program, BEST, delivered online, adapts the Buddhist Four Immeasurables practice to cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Ninety full-time doctors will be randomized to the program or a waitlist, completing surveys and giving blood samples at the start, middle, and end. Perceived stress is the main outcome, with burnout, depression, well-being, and sleep also tracked, with blood inflammation markers adding a hard-data layer. The design also tests what carries any benefit, measuring compassion, positive affect, equanimity, and mindfulness as candidate carriers. A positive-emotion focus, they hope, proves stronger medicine than attention training alone.
plos-pone-0359206:
Kathryn Date and eight colleagues published this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes the CONIFAS2 study, a feasibility test of a nature-based intervention for children with ADHD. The intervention was co-produced, designed together with the people who would use it.

A feasibility study asks whether a bigger trial can work at all: will families join, stay, and accept the activities? Nature-based activities are a low-drug option many families welcome, but they still need proper testing. Researchers planning the full trial, and clinicians who advise families with ADHD, are the readers for this groundwork.
plos-pone-0359306:
Monique Bussmann, Marieke Groot, Chris Kuiper, and Mieke Cardol published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is an ethnographic multi-case study of musical encounters in healthcare, moments when music is brought to patients. The authors call these encounters precarious, valuable yet fragile, and explore why.

Perspectives come from both care professionals and the musicians themselves, whose views of the same visit can differ sharply. shaku-sermons-buddhist-abbot-1906:

sinclair-jungle-1906:

W. Warde Fowler, an Oxford historian, asked in The Religious Experience of the Roman People what religion actually felt like to ordinary Romans. Household gods at the hearth, festivals marking the farming year, vows in sickness and danger, and the dread of getting a ritual word wrong make up his subject. Rome's faith was practice more than belief.

Delivered as Gifford Lectures, the study is scholarly but humane, resisting both mockery of superstition and romantic overreading. Fowler follows Roman religion from the early republic's calendar to the empire's encounter with Eastern cults and Christianity. Readers get ancient Rome's inner life respectfully reconstructed, a corrective to histories that count only legions, laws, and emperors.
tob-4306:
Moses Maimonides, the great Jewish thinker of the twelfth century, wrote his Guide for readers torn between the Torah and Greek philosophy. Many educated Jews felt that faith and reason pulled against each other. In M. Friedlander's English translation, the Guide speaks directly to that conflict.

Maimonides treats hard questions one by one: what words about God can truly mean, whether the world was created, and how prophecy works. He reads Scripture with care and argues that reason, used well, supports faith rather than destroying it. Few medieval books have been debated so long or so fiercely.
tourneur-revengers-tragedy-1606:
Printed in 1607 with no author's name, The Revenger's Tragedy was long credited to Cyril Tourneur. Most scholars now assign it to Thomas Middleton instead. Vindice, the lead figure, has spent nine years grieving for his murdered love, and he returns to court in disguise carrying her skull.

The court he enters is ruled by a lecherous Duke and a brood of grasping sons and stepsons. Plot piles on plot until revenge turns into a bloody masque of killing. Dark wit runs through every scene, and the mix of horror and sharp talk has made the play a lasting landmark of Jacobean drama.
un-ga-res-106:
Armenian deaths under the Ottoman Empire stand at the heart of the text filed here as Resolution 106. The file is not a UN text at all. It is a resolution of the U.S. House of Representatives, H. Res. 106 of the 110th Congress, sent to committee on 30 January 2007. It calls on the President to make sure that U.S. foreign dealings show due grasp of the facts on human rights, ethnic cleansing, and genocide in the U.S. record on the Armenian Genocide.

Adam Schiff led the sponsors of the text, with men of both parties beside him. The short name is given in full: the Affirmation of the United States Record on the Armenian Genocide Resolution. Fights over such texts, and over the word genocide itself, marked U.S. and Turkish ties for years. The catalog's UN label and 1915 year are both wrong.
un-sc-res-106:
Resolution 106 condemns an attack by Israeli regular army forces on Egyptian forces in the Gaza Strip on 28 February 1955. The catalog record dates the entry 1948, but the text itself was adopted on 29 March 1955, by a unanimous vote. An Egypt-Israel armistice panel had found the attack was planned and ordered by Israeli authorities.

The Council calls the attack a breach of the cease-fire terms in Resolution 54 and of the General Armistice Agreement between Egypt and Israel. It calls on Israel to take all steps needed to stop such actions. It also warns that any willful breach of the armistice puts the deal at risk, and that no real peace in Palestine can come unless both sides keep their word.
un-sc-res-1306:
Rough diamonds from Sierra Leone were banned from world markets on 5 July 2000. The Council voiced concern at the part played by the illegal diamond trade in fueling the war. Such stones were reported to pass through neighboring countries, Liberia among them. The diamond industry and West African states were already working on the trade's openness.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ordered all states to bar the direct or indirect import of rough diamonds from Sierra Leone. The ban would run for an initial eighteen months. One door stayed open: stones covered by a certificate of origin scheme run by Sierra Leone's government were exempt. Freetown was told to set that scheme up as a matter of urgency and to tell the sanctions committee. States and bodies were asked to help it do so. The move was an early step toward the global Kimberley controls on conflict diamonds.
un-sc-res-1406: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 1406, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 2002. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1506:
Libya's long isolation ended at the United Nations with Resolution 1506, adopted in September 2003. Sanctions placed on Tripoli after the Lockerbie bombing had been suspended for years. Once Libya accepted responsibility terms and a settlement, the Council lifted the measures for good.

Inside the short text, the members remove the arms and travel bans and close the sanctions committee's work. The vote closed a dispute that had run since the 1980s over the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103. It remains the formal end of one of the UN's longest sanctions cases.
un-sc-res-1606: Security Council Resolution 1606 is preserved here from the UN's official record, in a transcription by English Wikisource. Resolutions like this one typically run a few pages: findings first, then a short list of decisions. The entry's completeness is its feature, giving the whole act rather than a headline version of what was decided.
un-sc-res-1706:
Darfur's suffering drove Resolution 1706, adopted in August 2006. The Council voted to expand the UN mission in Sudan to take over from African Union troops in Darfur. Sudan's government, however, refused to accept the deployment, setting up a long standoff.

The text details a force of more than 17,000 soldiers plus police, tasked with protecting civilians and guarding the Darfur peace deal. Because Khartoum blocked it, the plan was later replaced by a joint UN-African Union mission. The resolution preserves the world's first full answer to Darfur, and the limits of voting without consent.
un-sc-res-1806: Resolution 1806, adopted in 2008, is a Security Council act preserved here through English Wikisource's transcription of the record. The number places it among the Council's 1800s run, the output of its later-2000s sessions. The entry gives the full decision at that place: grounds, orders, and the reporting follow-through that such texts standardly require.
un-sc-res-1906:
By Resolution 1906, adopted on 23 December 2009, the Council acted on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Militias in the east still preyed on civilians. Sexual violence, child soldier use, and summary killings went unpunished. The peacekeeping mission faced hard questions about its future shape and size.

The Council extends the mission, called MONUC, until 31 May 2010, keeping up to 19,815 troops. Guarding civilians ranks first among its duties. Joint protection teams and early warning posts, tested in North Kivu, should spread to the south. The Secretary-General must deliver a strategic review by 1 April 2010. It will set out what must be done before any drawdown can start safely.
un-sc-res-206:
A thin calm held in Cyprus in the summer of 1965, and the Secretary-General warned it might not last without the peacekeeping force. His report recommended keeping the force for six more months. Cyprus's government wanted it to stay beyond 26 June 1965. Resolution 206 was adopted unanimously on 15 June 1965.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General and the states that sent troops, police, supplies, and money. Its earlier Cyprus resolutions were reaffirmed. The parties were called on to keep showing restraint and to cooperate fully with the force. The force's stationing was extended for six months, ending on 26 December 1965. The longer term matched the warning in the report. A fresh outbreak of fighting was feared if the force left too soon.
un-sc-res-406:
Botswana's call for help was answered on 25 May 1977. The Council had the report of the mission it sent under resolution 403 (1977). Botswana's foreign minister described continued attacks and provocations by the Rhodesian regime. The Secretary-General had written to all states on 18 April with the mission's findings. Solidarity with Botswana was judged essential to solving the Rhodesia question.

The Council voiced full support for Botswana's government as it guarded the country's sovereignty and independence. It thanked the Secretary-General for sending the mission. The mission's assessment and recommendations were endorsed in full. His April appeal to all states, asking urgent financial and material help for Botswana, won the Council's full backing as well. A special account at Headquarters, opened to receive gifts for Botswana, was welcomed. United Nations bodies were asked to act on the mission's plan, and states holding aid back were pressed to respond.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 106, adopted unanimously on 29 March 1955, condemns an Israeli attack in the Gaza Strip. The Council had heard the report of the Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. It had heard statements by Egypt and Israel. It notes the finding of the Egyptian-Israel Mixed Armistice Commission of 6 March 1955.

The Commission had determined that the attack of 28 February 1955 was a prearranged and planned attack. It was ordered by the Israeli authorities. It was carried out by regular army forces against an Egyptian regular army force in Gaza. The Council condemns it as a violation of the cease-fire set by resolution 54 (1948) and of the General Armistice Agreement. It calls again on Israel to prevent such actions. It warns that deliberate violations threaten the armistice system. Any return to permanent peace in Palestine depends on that system.

Blood diamonds are targeted in Resolution 1306, adopted on 5 July 2000. The Council said it was troubled by the role of the illicit diamond trade in fueling Sierra Leone's war, since rebels sold rough stones, often through Liberia, to buy weapons. It also stressed that the legitimate diamond trade matters greatly to many economies and can aid recovery when it is clean.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council banned the direct and indirect import of rough diamonds from Sierra Leone unless they moved under a certificate-of-origin regime controlled by Sierra Leone's government. The ban ran for an initial eighteen months. The scheme helped invent the global certification system later embodied in the Kimberley Process.

More time to study a report is the whole point here. On 30 April 2002 the Council extended MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 31 July 2002. The pause let members weigh the Secretary-General's report of 19 February 2002 on the territory's future, while the Western Sahara question stayed under the Council's review.

Sanctions imposed on Libya over the Lockerbie and UTA flight bombings are lifted on 12 September 2003. The measures dated from the early 1990s. Libya had now written to the Council accepting responsibility for its officials' actions, paying compensation, renouncing terrorism, and promising cooperation with further inquiries.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ended the sanctions with immediate effect. It dissolved the sanctions committee that had overseen them since 1992. It also closed its handling of the whole item, removing it from the list of matters before it. The vote was 13 in favour and none against, with France and the United States abstaining.

A truth and justice process for Burundi's past crimes is opened up on 20 June 2005. Burundi's government had asked in 2002, under the Arusha Agreement, for an international judicial commission of inquiry. A report sent to the Council in March 2005 set out recommendations for handling that request.

Lasting peace, the Council says, requires establishing the truth about genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes committed in Burundi since independence, and bringing those most responsible to justice. The Secretary-General is asked to open negotiations with Burundi's government. He is also to consult all Burundian parties on how to carry out his recommendations, with a report on those talks due by 30 September 2005.

Expanding the Sudan mission into Darfur is decided on 31 August 2006. The African Union force in Darfur was overstretched, and the Council had resolved in May to move toward a United Nations operation there. Sudan's sovereignty, it is stressed, would be unaffected by the transition, and the Darfur peace agreement is pressed to be carried out.

UNMIS is to be strengthened by up to 17,300 military personnel and a large civilian police component for Darfur. The Secretary-General is asked to arrange rapid deployment of extra resources and to consult jointly with the African Union on the handover. The expanded mission's tasks in Darfur include protecting civilians, watching the ceasefire, and supporting the peace deal, though Sudan's consent remained a live dispute.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended for another year on 20 March 2008. The Afghanistan Compact remained the shared framework for security, governance, and development, owned by Afghans themselves. The linked fight against the drug trade, which funded the insurgency and corruption alike, is also noted.

UNAMA's mandate, as defined in earlier resolutions, is renewed, and its coordination role across the country is strengthened. The mission and its head are to lead world civilian efforts, support the government's development strategy, and help deliver aid and protection. All Afghan and international actors are called on to work with the mission, and the government is urged to deepen reform, above all in security and justice.

MONUC is extended for five months while its future shape is studied in Resolution 1906, adopted on 23 December 2009. Militias in eastern Congo had still not disarmed. Targeted attacks, sexual violence, and child recruitment continued. Relations with neighbouring states were improving under regional agreements.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 31 May 2010 at up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. It signals a further twelve months after that. The Secretary-General must deliver a strategic review by 1 April 2010, with benchmarks, reconfiguration options, and the critical tasks to finish before drawdown. MONUC's priorities are fixed in order: protect civilians, run disarmament and demobilization for Congolese and foreign armed groups, and support security sector reform. North Kivu protection tools such as Joint Protection Teams and Early Warning Centres must be extended, especially to South Kivu.

Resolution 206 is a UN Security Council renewal for Cyprus, adopted unanimously on 15 June 1965. The Secretary-General recommended keeping the peacekeeping force for six months this time, longer than the usual three, and the government of Cyprus asked for the deployment to continue past late June.

His report warned that the island's quiet was tenuous and that fighting would very likely resume early if the force withdrew. The Council therefore kept the peacekeepers in place and restated its appreciation to the Secretary-General and the states backing the mission. The doubled extension length shows the Council accepting, by mid-1965, that Cyprus needed a longer commitment rather than emergency stopgaps.

Choosing a Secretary-General is the sole purpose of Resolution 306, adopted unanimously on 21 December 1971. The Council had considered whom to recommend as the United Nations' top official. U Thant of Burma was stepping down after a decade in the job, and governments had settled on an Austrian diplomat and former foreign minister as his successor.

In one sentence, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that Kurt Waldheim be appointed Secretary-General. The Charter splits this choice in two: the Assembly appoints, but only someone the Council has put forward. Waldheim went on to serve two terms through 1981, and his tenure later drew scrutiny over his wartime record, which makes this brief appointment text a document historians still revisit.

Resolution 406 passed with no vote on 25 May 1977. It turns a fact-finding trip into real aid for Botswana. A UN team sent months before had sized up Botswana's needs. Rhodesia's white-led regime kept up raids and taunts across the border. Botswana's foreign chief told the Council of the harm in the hall. The UN chief had called on all states in April to stand with Botswana, a small state in the front line of the Rhodesia fight.

The Council voiced full faith in Botswana's right to guard its land, its borders, and its free rule. It backed the UN team's findings and its plan in full. It backed the call for aid just as fully. The aid aimed at roads, water, and farms, so Botswana could stand firm.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The tenth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/6406, covers the force in 1965 and 1966. UNEF was nearing a full decade on the Egypt-Israel frontier. Few at its birth in the Suez Crisis had expected so long a stay, and its costs drew steady debate.

The report reviews patrols, incidents, troop strength, and the force's budget. It records a quiet border and a mission in working order. It is the last full report in the run: the force was pulled out in May 1967, and war followed within weeks.
virginia-charter-1606:
King James I granted the First Charter of Virginia in 1606 to a group of London merchants and gentlemen. Their company planned to plant an English colony on the coast of North America. The charter gave them legal cover to sail, settle, and govern under English law.

The text sets the colony's borders, names its ruling councils, and promises settlers the rights of English subjects. It also claims rights to mine gold, silver, and copper, sharing a part with the crown. A year later the company's colonists founded Jamestown. The charter is thus a founding paper of English America.
wieger-textes-philosophiques-1906:
Léon Wieger, a French Jesuit who spent his life in China, gathered these Chinese philosophical texts in 1906 and presented them in French. Wieger ran a mission press in Hebei and became known for exact work on Chinese language and thought. His aim was to let French readers meet China's sages in their own words.

The chosen pieces span schools and ages, from early masters to later teachers of the Way and of Confucius. Short lives and notes help the reader place each text. Wieger's versions were trusted for their care, and the set still serves as a window on how Europe first read Chinese thought in depth.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol06:
In 1859 Volume VI of the Journal of Discourses added another year of preaching to the printed record. Liverpool remained the printing base for a Utah church speaking to a worldwide flock. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles fill the pages, their sermons taken down word for word.

The talks show doctrine being worked out in public, applied to marriages, farms, debts, and doubts. That mix of the sacred and the everyday is the Journal's signature across all twenty-six volumes. Volume VI, read in sequence, lets the movement's teaching be watched as it grows.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-1-1906:
The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the central work of the Kabbalah, ascribed to the circle of Moses de Leon in thirteenth-century Spain. It reads the Torah as a map of the hidden life of God, in the form of talks among Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions. Jean de Pauly turned the whole work into French, and his first tome appeared in 1906. No complete English version in the public domain exists.

The opening tomes follow Genesis, verse by verse turned to mystery: the ten sefirot, the letters of creation, and the souls of the patriarchs. De Pauly's French is the only complete public domain rendering of the whole Zohar. His six tomes made the book open to Western readers.
